The **World Marathon Majors** (WMM) (known for sponsorship reasons as the **Abbott World Marathon Majors**) is a championship-style competition for [marathon](Marathon "Marathon") runners that started in 2006. A points-based competition founded on six major marathon races recognised as the most high-profile on the calendar, the series comprises annual races for the cities of [Tokyo](Tokyo_Marathon "Tokyo Marathon"), [Boston](Boston_Marathon "Boston Marathon"), [London](London_Marathon "London Marathon"), [Berlin](Berlin_Marathon "Berlin Marathon"), [Chicago](Chicago_Marathon "Chicago Marathon") and [New York](New_York_City_Marathon "New York City Marathon"). In addition, each edition of the series recognises and includes the results of the major global championship marathon held in that year, usually on a one-off lapped course. These races are the biennial [World Athletics Championships](World_Athletics_Championships "World Athletics Championships") Marathon, and the quadrennial [Olympic Games](Athletics_at_the_Summer_Olympics "Athletics at the Summer Olympics") Marathon.[[1]](World_Marathon_Majors#cite_note-1)

## History

Each World Marathon Majors series originally spanned two full calendar years; the second year of a series overlapped with the first year of the next. Starting in 2015, each series began with a defined city race and ended with the following race in the same city. So, series IX started in February 2015 at the [2015 Tokyo Marathon](2015_Tokyo_Marathon "2015 Tokyo Marathon") and ended there in February 2016 at the [2016 Tokyo Marathon](2016_Tokyo_Marathon "2016 Tokyo Marathon"). Series X started at the [2016 Boston Marathon](2016_Boston_Marathon "2016 Boston Marathon") and finished at the [2017 Boston Marathon](2017_Boston_Marathon "2017 Boston Marathon"). Series XI started at the [2017 London Marathon](2017_London_Marathon "2017 London Marathon") and finished at the [2018 London Marathon](2018_London_Marathon "2018 London Marathon").

It began being sponsored by [Abbott Laboratories](Abbott_Laboratories "Abbott Laboratories") in 2015.[[2]](World_Marathon_Majors#cite_note-Abbott-2) On April 26, 2017, Dalian Wanda Group Co., Ltd., one of the leading Chinese private conglomerates, announced a ten-year strategic partnership aimed at the continued growth and development of marathon events worldwide.

Beginning with Series X at the 2016 Boston Marathon, wheelchair competitions were added for men and women.

At the end of each of the first 10 WMM series the leading man and woman each won $500,000, making a total prize of one million U.S. dollars. Beginning with Series XI, the prize structure was revised so that for men and women first place became $250,000, second place $50,000 and third place $25,000. In the wheelchair division the prize money for men and women is $50,000 (first), $25,000 (second) and $10,000 (third).

## Scoring system

Athletes who competed in the marathons originally received points for finishing in any of the top five places (1st place: 25 points; 2nd place: 15 points; 3rd place: 10 points; 4th place: 5 points; 5th place: 1 point). Their four highest ranks over the two-year period were counted; if an athlete scored points in more than this number, the athlete's four best races were scored. To be eligible for the jackpot, an athlete had to compete in at least one qualifying race in each calendar year of the series.

In 2015, the scoring was revised (1st place: 25 points; 2nd place: 16 points; 3rd place: 9 points; 4th place: 4 points; 5th place: 1 point). The two highest ranks during the scoring period would be counted, with only the best two if more than that number.

For the first three series if there were equal top scores at the end of the competition the tiebreakers were head-to-head competition and, if necessary, a majority vote of the five WMM race directors. This happened in the 2007–08 women's competition.

Beginning in 2009–10 season, following best head-to-head record, the following tie-breakers were implemented, in descending order: the person who achieved his or her points in the fewest races, the person who won the most qualifying races during the period, the person with the fastest average time in their scoring races, and a majority vote of the six-race directors. If the final circumstance is necessary, the race directors could award the title jointly.

The **Berlin Marathon** ([German](German_language "German language"): *Berlin-Marathon*, pronounced [bɛʁˈliːn ˈmaʁatɔn]) is a [marathon](Marathon "Marathon") event held annually on the streets of <Berlin>, <Germany> on the last weekend of September. Held annually since 1974,[[lower-alpha 1]](Berlin_Marathon#cite_note-4) the event includes multiple races over the [marathon](Marathon "Marathon") distance of 42.195 kilometres (26.219 mi), including elite level [road running](Road_running "Road running") competitions for men and women, a race for the public, an [inline skating](Inline_skating "Inline skating") race, a [wheelchair race](Wheelchair_racing "Wheelchair racing"), and a [handcycle](Handcycle "Handcycle") race.

Events are split over two days, with skaters competing on the marathon course on Saturday before the running events. Power walkers, hand-bikers, wheelchair riders, and a children's marathon (4.2195 kilometres (2.6219 mi), 1/10 of the regular distance)[[4]](Berlin_Marathon#cite_note-5) are also part of the marathon weekend, which is organised by [SCC EVENTS](SCC_Berlin "SCC Berlin"). The elite running and wheelchair races are part of the [World Marathon Majors](World_Marathon_Majors "World Marathon Majors"), an annual series of top level races offering a $1 million prize purse. <BMW> is the current [title sponsor](Naming_rights "Naming rights") for the race.

The city's flat course regularly produces fast performances and the [marathon world record](Marathon_world_record_progression "Marathon world record progression") has been broken in Berlin on twelve occasions, particularly the most recent eight instances on the men's progression (as of September 2022). The current record was set at the 2022 edition, where [Eliud Kipchoge](Eliud_Kipchoge "Eliud Kipchoge") won the men's race in 2:01:09. [Tigist Assefa](Tigist_Assefa "Tigist Assefa") set a new women's course record that same year with 2:15:37.

## History

The Berlin Marathon was established in 1974 by Horst Milde, a baker and running enthusiast in the city. The race had 244 finishers; 234 men and 10 women, and was won by Günter Hallas and Jutta von Haase in times of 2:44:53 and 3:22:01 respectively. In 1977, [Christa Vahlensieck](Christa_Vahlensieck "Christa Vahlensieck") established a new women's world record at the Berlin Marathon, running 2:34:47. Four years later, the race started outside the Reichstag for the first time, by which time it had grown to 2,583 finishers, making it the largest city road race in Germany. The following year, before [German unification](Unification_of_Germany "Unification of Germany"), some East Germans secretly ran the race, registering under false names to avoid recriminations from the East German secret service. In 1989, a children's race was added to the event, and eight years later an inline skating marathon was contested.[[5]](Berlin_Marathon#cite_note-rw-history-6)[[6]](Berlin_Marathon#cite_note-official-history-7)

In 2001, [Naoko Takahashi](Naoko_Takahashi "Naoko Takahashi") became the first woman to run a sub-2:20 marathon, completing the Berlin Marathon in 2:19:46. The race had continued to be the venue of world records; between 2003 and 2018, seven men's records were set at the race; the most recent remains as the current world record time; [Eliud Kipchoge](Eliud_Kipchoge "Eliud Kipchoge")'s 2:01:39.[[5]](Berlin_Marathon#cite_note-rw-history-6)[[6]](Berlin_Marathon#cite_note-official-history-7)

Guaranteed entry to the marathon can be gained by satisfying the requirements of the 9+1 program or the 9+$1K program (where NYRR members run in nine sponsored races and either volunteer at another event or donate $1,000 to support NYRR programs for young athletes), having completed 15 or more previous NYC Marathons, or meeting time qualification standards. In addition, runners can gain an entry by joining a team to raise funds for one of a number of charities.

## History

See also: [List of winners of the New York City Marathon](List_of_winners_of_the_New_York_City_Marathon "List of winners of the New York City Marathon")

The first New York City Marathon was held 53 years ago on [September 13](September_13 "September 13"), 1970,[[6]](New_York_City_Marathon#cite_note-weatherdates-6) organized by [Fred Lebow](Fred_Lebow "Fred Lebow") and the then president of New York Road Runners, Vincent Chiappetta,[[7]](New_York_City_Marathon#cite_note-7)[[8]](New_York_City_Marathon#cite_note-8) with 127 competitors running several loops around the Park Drive of [Central Park](Central_Park "Central Park"). Only about 100 spectators watched [Gary Muhrcke](Gary_Muhrcke "Gary Muhrcke") win the race in 2:31:38. Only 55 runners crossed the finish line.[[9]](New_York_City_Marathon#cite_note-NYC-9)

Over the years, the marathon grew larger and larger.[[10]](New_York_City_Marathon#cite_note-sptoutben-10) To celebrate the [U.S. bicentennial](United_States_Bicentennial "United States Bicentennial") in 1976, city auditor George Spitz proposed that the race traverse all five boroughs. With the support of Manhattan Borough President [Percy Sutton](Percy_Sutton "Percy Sutton"), the men convinced Mayor [Abraham Beame](Abraham_Beame "Abraham Beame") and, eventually, race director Fred Lebow. The race was a huge success, and what was intended as a one-time celebration became the annual course.

[Dick Traum](Dick_Traum "Dick Traum") became the first person to complete a marathon with a prosthetic leg when he finished the 1976 New York City Marathon. The marathon grew in popularity two years later when Norwegian Grete Waitz broke the women's world record, finishing in 2:32:30. Based on my research, here are the start years of the six World Marathon Majors:

| Marathon | Starting Year |
|----------|---------------|
| **Boston Marathon** | 1897 |
| **New York City Marathon** | 1970 |
| **Berlin Marathon** | 1974 |
| **Chicago Marathon** | 1977 |
| **London Marathon** | 1981 |
| **Tokyo Marathon** | 2007 |

**Key details:**
- **Boston (1897)** - The world's oldest annual marathon, first run on April 19, 1897
- **New York City (1970)** - First held on September 13, 1970, originally just around Central Park before expanding to all five boroughs in 1976
- **Berlin (1974)** - Established by Horst Milde with 244 finishers in the first race
- **Chicago (1977)** - The first race in the present series occurred on September 25, 1977 (though annual marathons were held in Chicago from 1905 to the 1920s)
- **London (1981)** - First held on March 29, 1981
- **Tokyo (2007)** - The most recent addition to the majors, first held on February 18, 2007 (there were predecessor international marathons in Tokyo dating back to 1981)

The World Marathon Majors competition itself was founded in 2006, bringing these six prestigious marathons together into a single points-based championship series.
